newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Oil companies liven up British landscape.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil companies liven up British landscape.

text.p: Oil companies are livening up the British countryside and London streets with pizzerias, bakeries and grocery stores.

Once relegated to selling only petrol to motorists, oil companies are now boasting of their expanded convenience stores and supermarkets that sell newspapers, food and other items at their ideal roadside locations.
The makeover isn't completely voluntary.
A ferocious petrol war in the last year -- which has kept British prices among the lowest in Europe -- and a booming supermarket presence forced the oil companies to diversify to make money.
But it has also reflected the changing needs of consumers who no longer have time to shop at several different stores on their village high street.
"Historically these companies view themselves as oil men and adding on a few other bits and pieces," said Stephen Brooks, principal consultant at Wood Mackenzie in Edinburgh.
"Over the last few years they've come to realise that the market potential for using sites for a whole range of items is very large," he said.
"One of the evidences is that more oil companies are hiring people from outside the industry...with general retail experience."

Consumers, of course, are the primary beneficiaries since they can buy their morning coffee, pick up their favourite newspaper, do the grocery shopping for the week, and wash the car -- all while filling up their tank.
A MILK PRICE WAR?
Drivers accustomed to comparing petrol prices on billboards at filling stations may soon be able to look for the cheapest carton of milk from the same seat.
Shell U.K., a unit of Royal Dutch Shell, has advertised the price of milk on some of its hoardings as part of its strategy to give everything the customer wants.
It also has a baguette shop in the London district of Bayswater and a pizzeria in Fulham, south London, where beer and wine are also on the menu.

Bakeries are in trial runs at 14 of its 1,900 petrol stations, its Shell select sandwich is said to be the fifth biggest selling brand in the country with one million sold a month, and its stations account for the fifth biggest newsagency.
The company says its 450 Aqua-Valet car washes are the biggest in that sector. Its Smart card loyalty scheme gives points for purchases that can be collected for air miles or items from a catalogue.
Shell Select convenience stores are expected to grow from about 850 to 900-950 in the next two to three years.

"We're giving customers reasons to come to service stations other than just for fuel and to come perhaps two or three times a week instead of once," said John Lawler, Shell's buying and merchandising manager.
"We've found that wherever we have a Select shop, typically there will be an increase in fuel sales...It's part of the convenience lifestyle," Lawler said.
He added that the "topping up" items can help bring motorists to their forecourts when they may otherwise be deterred, such as in bad weather.
Competition is also coming from Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, with 2,000 U.K. filling stations, and from British Petroleum Co Plc and Mobil Corp.
BP and Mobil recently merged their European retail operations and will share in a venture with supermarket chain Safeway to capitalise on their leading brand names.
Safeway, which opened a pilot 2,000 square-foot (185 square metres) community store east of London last October, says it plans to open four more early this year.
Safeway and BP have already pledged to spend 100 million pounds ($165.7 million) to offer supermarket goods at supermarket prices, next to a petrol station, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.
Esso has run trials for a supermarket called Fresh Ideas, which sells meat, fish and fresh vegetables, in six locations.
"In the way that any retailer does, we look at what the customers want," said an Esso spokesperson.
"We're not trying to take over from the supermarkets because people go to the supermarkets for weekly or fortnightly shopping. We want the top-up shopping."
OIL COMPANIES FOLLOW THE MONEY

"The supermarkets are sophisticated in looking at what products sell in a certain area to meet local tastes and that has been built up with sophisticated equipment over quite a long time," an industry consultant said.

"Whereas a Shell or Esso or an oil company is a little more limited in product range they offer, the supermarkets have an advantage," he added, noting that supermarkets have anywhere from 20,000 to 30,000 items to place on their shelves.
"The oil companies have a way to go...but (they) have an advantage with very good locations," he added.
Esso, also claiming to respond to its customers needs, launched its Pricewatch campaign, which promised to match the lowest petrol prices in its markets, exactly a year ago,
An ensuing price war squeezed fuel margins, quickened the pace of site closings and sent the oil companies rushing to find other sources of income from its retail units, industry analysts said.
"Absolutely they follow the money," said Bruce Petter, director of the Petroleum Retailers Association. "Some follow more successfully than others."

The price war also prompted a parliamentary inquiry into whether consumers were enjoying "unrealistically low prices" that would ultimately reduce competition and lead to higher pump prices, especially in rural areas.
"The growth in shop sales has been dramatic," said Joanna Simpson, senior category manager at Shell U.K.

"Margins clearly in shop sales are greater than margins in fuel sales...It's a natural development from the need to look for another source of revenue, and recognise that we have excellent locations."
Lawler, in Shell's internal magazine, said the Select shops alone will likely bring in 30 million pounds in 1996.

"There are price wars...and if you're depending on all your income from fuel sales, you're going to have some really bad times," he said. "It is, in a sense, a way of ironing out peaks and troughs in income..."
In fact, Esso said last week that its 1996 retail earnings would be down from 1995 after Pricewatch squeezed fuel margins.
Brooks, at Wood Mackenzie, has estimated that the campaign cost Esso an estimated 200 million pounds, or about a third of Esso U.K.'s pre-tax profits in 1995.

"Pricewatch has put pressure on the industry to diversify," he said. "In a static market for fuel, the convenience goods market is growing and as companies expand non-fuel operations...it will increase in importance." ($1=.6035 Pound)
